{{Short description|Operator generalizing the Laplacian in differential geometry}}
{{Distinguish|Beltrami operator}}
In [[differential geometry]], the '''Laplace–Beltrami operator''' is a generalization of the [[Laplace operator]] to functions defined on [[submanifold]]s in [[Euclidean space]] and, even more generally, on [[Riemannian manifold|Riemannian]] and [[pseudo-Riemannian manifold]]s. It is named after [[Pierre-Simon Laplace]] and [[Eugenio Beltrami]].

For any twice-[[differentiable function|differentiable]] real-valued function ''f'' defined on Euclidean space '''R'''<sup>''n''</sup>, the Laplace operator (also known as the ''Laplacian'') takes ''f'' to the [[divergence]] of its [[gradient]] vector field, which is the sum of the ''n'' pure second derivatives of ''f'' with respect to each vector of an [[orthonormal basis]] for '''R'''<sup>''n''</sup>. Like the Laplacian, the Laplace–Beltrami operator is defined as the divergence of the gradient, and is a [[linear operator]] taking functions into functions. The operator can be extended to operate on tensors as the divergence of the covariant derivative. Alternatively, the operator can be generalized to operate on [[differential form]]s using the divergence and [[exterior derivative]]. The resulting operator is called the Laplace–de Rham operator (named after [[Georges de Rham]]).

==Details==
The Laplace–Beltrami operator, like the Laplacian, is the (Riemannian) [[divergence]] of the (Riemannian) [[gradient]]:
:<math>\Delta f = {\rm div}( \nabla f).</math>
An explicit formula in [[local coordinates]] is possible.

Suppose first that ''M'' is an [[oriented manifold|oriented]] [[Riemannian manifold]]. The orientation allows one to specify a definite [[volume form]] on ''M'', given in an oriented coordinate system ''x''<sup>''i''</sup> by

:<math>\operatorname{vol}_n := \sqrt{|g|} \;dx^1\wedge \cdots \wedge dx^n</math>

where {{nowrap|1={{!}}''g''{{!}} := {{!}}det(''g<sub>ij</sub>''){{!}}}} is the [[absolute value]] of the [[determinant]] of the [[metric tensor]], and the ''dx<sup>i</sup>'' are the [[1-form]]s forming the [[coframe|dual frame]] to the frame
:<math>\partial_i := \frac {\partial}{\partial x^i}</math>
of the [[tangent bundle]] <math>TM</math> and <math>\wedge</math> is the [[wedge product]].

The divergence of a vector field <math>X</math> on the manifold is then defined as the scalar function <math>\nabla \cdot X</math> with the property

:<math>
(\nabla \cdot X) \operatorname{vol}_n := L_X \operatorname{vol}_n
</math>

where ''L<sub>X</sub>'' is the [[Lie derivative]] along the [[vector field]] ''X''. In local coordinates, one obtains

:<math>
\nabla \cdot X = \frac{1}{\sqrt{|g|}} \partial_i \left(\sqrt {|g|} X^i\right)
</math>

where here and below the [[Einstein notation]] is implied, so that the repeated index ''i'' is summed over.
 
The gradient of a scalar function ƒ is the vector field grad ''f'' that may be defined through the [[inner product]] <math>\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle</math> on the manifold, as

:<math>\langle \operatorname{grad} f(x) , v_x \rangle = df(x)(v_x)</math>

for all vectors ''v<sub>x</sub>'' anchored at point ''x'' in the [[tangent space]] ''T<sub>x</sub>M'' of the manifold at point ''x''.  Here, ''d''ƒ is the [[exterior derivative]] of the function ƒ; it is a 1-form taking argument ''v<sub>x</sub>''. In local coordinates, one has

:<math> \left(\operatorname{grad} f\right)^i = 
\partial^i f = g^{ij} \partial_j f</math>

where ''g<sup>ij</sup>'' are the components of the inverse of the [[metric tensor]], so that {{nowrap|1=''g<sup>ij</sup>g<sub>jk</sub>'' = &delta;<sup>''i''</sup><sub>''k''</sub>}} with δ<sup>''i''</sup><sub>''k''</sub> the [[Kronecker delta]].

Combining the definitions of the gradient and divergence, the formula for the Laplace–Beltrami operator applied to a scalar function ƒ is, in local coordinates

:<math>\Delta  f = \frac{1}{\sqrt {|g|}} \partial_i \left(\sqrt{|g|} g^{ij} \partial_j f \right).</math>

If ''M'' is not oriented, then the above calculation carries through exactly as presented, except that the volume form must instead be replaced by a [[volume element]] (a [[density on a manifold|density]] rather than a form).  Neither the gradient nor the divergence actually depends on the choice of orientation, and so the Laplace–Beltrami operator itself does not depend on this additional structure.

==Formal self-adjointness==

The exterior derivative <math>d</math> and <math>- \nabla</math> are formal adjoints, in the sense that for a compactly supported function <math>f</math>

:<math>\int_M df(X) \operatorname{vol}_n = - \int_M f  \nabla \cdot X \operatorname{vol}_n </math>

where the last equality is an application of [[Stokes' theorem]].  Dualizing gives

{{NumBlk|:|<math>\int_M f \,\Delta  h\,\operatorname{vol}_n = -\int_M \langle df, dh\rangle\, \operatorname{vol}_n</math>|{{EquationRef|2}}}}

for all compactly supported functions <math>f</math> and <math>h</math>.  Conversely, ({{EquationRef|2}}) characterizes the Laplace–Beltrami operator completely, in the sense that it is the only operator with this property.

As a consequence, the Laplace–Beltrami operator is negative and formally self-adjoint, meaning that for compactly supported functions <math>f</math> and <math>h</math>,

:<math>\int_M f\,\Delta  h \operatorname{vol}_n = -\int_M \langle d f, d h \rangle \operatorname{vol}_n = \int_M h\,\Delta  f \operatorname{vol}_n.</math>

Because the Laplace–Beltrami operator, as defined in this manner, is negative rather than positive, often it is defined with the opposite sign.

==Eigenvalues of the Laplace–Beltrami operator (Lichnerowicz–Obata theorem)==
Let M denote a compact Riemannian manifold without boundary. We want to consider the eigenvalue equation,
:<math> -\Delta  u=\lambda u,</math>
where <math>u</math> is the [[eigenfunction]] associated with the eigenvalue <math>\lambda</math>. It can be shown using the self-adjointness proved above that the eigenvalues <math>\lambda</math> are real. The compactness of the manifold <math>M</math> allows one to show that the eigenvalues are discrete and furthermore, the [[vector space]] of eigenfunctions associated with a given eigenvalue <math>\lambda</math>, i.e. the [[eigenspace]]s are all finite-dimensional. Notice by taking the [[constant function]] as an eigenfunction, we get <math>\lambda=0</math> is an eigenvalue. Also since we have considered <math>-\Delta </math> an integration by parts shows that <math>\lambda\geq 0</math>. More precisely if we multiply the eigenvalue equation through by the eigenfunction <math>u</math> and integrate the resulting equation on <math>M</math> we get (using the notation <math>dV=\operatorname{vol}_n</math>):
:<math>-\int_M \Delta  u\ u\ dV=\lambda\int_Mu^2\ dV</math>
Performing an integration by parts or what is the same thing as using the [[divergence theorem]] on the term on the left, and since <math>M</math> has no boundary we get
:<math>-\int_M\Delta  u\ u\ dV=\int_M|\nabla u|^2\ dV</math>
Putting the last two equations together we arrive at
:<math>\int_M|\nabla u|^2\ dV=\lambda\int_Mu^2\ dV</math>
We conclude from the last equation that <math>\lambda\geq 0</math>.

A fundamental result of [[André Lichnerowicz]]<ref>{{cite book|author=Lichnerowicz, Andre|title=Geometrie des groupes de transformations|year=1958|publisher=Dunod|location=Paris}}</ref> states that: Given a compact ''n''-dimensional Riemannian manifold with no boundary with <math>n\geq 2</math>. Assume the [[Ricci curvature]] satisfies the lower bound:
:<math> \operatorname{Ric}(X,X)\geq \kappa g(X,X),\kappa>0,</math>
where <math>g(\cdot,\cdot)</math> is the metric tensor and <math>X</math> is any tangent vector on the manifold <math>M</math>. Then the first positive eigenvalue <math>\lambda_1</math> of the eigenvalue equation satisfies the lower bound:
:<math> \lambda_1\geq \frac{n}{n-1}\kappa.</math>
This lower bound is sharp and achieved on the sphere <math>\mathbb{S}^n</math>. In fact on <math>\mathbb{S}^2</math> the eigenspace for <math>\lambda_1</math> is three dimensional and spanned by the restriction of the coordinate functions <math>x_1,x_2,x_3</math> from <math>\mathbb{R}^3</math> to <math>\mathbb{S}^2</math>. Using spherical coordinates <math>(\theta,\phi)</math>, on <math>\mathbb{S}^2</math> the two dimensional sphere, set
:<math>x_3=\cos\phi=u_1,</math>
we see easily from the formula for the spherical Laplacian displayed below that
:<math> -\Delta _{\mathbb{S}^2}u_1=2u_1</math>
Thus the lower bound in Lichnerowicz's theorem is achieved at least in two dimensions.

Conversely it was proved by [[Morio Obata]],<ref>{{cite journal|author=Obata, Morio|title=Certain conditions for a Riemannian manifold to be isometric with a sphere|journal=J. Math. Soc. Jpn.|volume=14|issue=3|year=1962|pages=333–340|doi=10.2969/jmsj/01430333|doi-access=free}}</ref> that if the ''n''-dimensional compact Riemannian manifold without boundary were such that for the first positive eigenvalue <math>\lambda_1</math> one has,
:<math>\lambda_1=\frac{n}{n-1}\kappa,</math>
then the manifold is isometric to the ''n''-dimensional sphere <math> \mathbb{S}^n\bigg(\sqrt{\frac{n-1}{\kappa}}\bigg)</math>, the sphere of radius <math>\sqrt{\frac{n-1}{\kappa}}</math>. Proofs of all these statements may be found in the book by Isaac Chavel.<ref>{{citation|first=Isaac|last=Chavel|title=Eigenvalues in Riemannian Geometry|publisher=Academic Press|year=1984|volume=115|edition=2nd|series=Pure and Applied Mathematics|isbn=978-0-12-170640-1}}</ref> Analogous sharp bounds also hold for other geometries and for certain degenerate Laplacians associated with these geometries like the [[CR manifold#The tangential Cauchy–Riemann complex (Kohn Laplacian, Kohn–Rossi complex)|Kohn Laplacian]] (after [[Joseph J. Kohn]]) on a compact [[CR manifold]]. Applications there are to the global embedding of such CR manifolds in <math>\mathbb{C}^n.</math><ref>{{cite journal|author=Chanillo, Sagun, Chiu, Hung-Lin and Yang, Paul C.|title=Embeddability for 3-dimensional CR manifolds and CR Yamabe Invariants|journal=Duke Mathematical Journal|volume=161|issue=15|year=2012|pages=2909–2921|doi=10.1215/00127094-1902154|arxiv=1007.5020|s2cid=304301}}</ref>

==Tensor Laplacian==

The Laplace–Beltrami operator can be written using the [[Tensor contraction|trace (or contraction)]] of the iterated [[covariant derivative]] associated with the [[Levi-Civita connection]]. The [[Hessian matrix#Generalizations to Riemannian manifolds|Hessian (tensor)]] of a function <math>f</math> is the symmetric 2-tensor

:<math>\displaystyle \mbox{Hess} f \in \mathbf \Gamma(\mathsf T^*M \otimes \mathsf T^*M),</math> <math>\mbox{Hess} f := \nabla^2 f \equiv \nabla \nabla f \equiv \nabla \mathrm df,</math>

where ''df'' denotes the [[Exterior derivative#Definition|(exterior) derivative]] of a function ''f''.

Let ''X''<sub>i</sub> be a basis of tangent vector fields (not necessarily induced by a coordinate system). Then the components of ''Hess f'' are given by

:<math>(\mbox{Hess} f)_{ij} = \mbox{Hess} f(X_i, X_j) = \nabla_{X_i}\nabla_{X_j} f - \nabla_{\nabla_{X_i}X_j} f</math>

This is easily seen to transform tensorially, since it is linear in each of the arguments ''X''<sub>i</sub>, ''X''<sub>j</sub>.  The Laplace–Beltrami operator is then the trace (or [[Tensor contraction|contraction]]) of the Hessian with respect to the metric:

:<math>\displaystyle \Delta f := \mathrm{tr} \nabla \mathrm df \in C^\infty(M).</math>

More precisely, this means

:<math>\displaystyle \Delta f(x) = \sum_{i=1}^n \nabla \mathrm df(X_i,X_i),</math>

or in terms of the metric

:<math>\Delta  f = \sum_{ij} g^{ij} (\mbox{Hess} f)_{ij}.</math>

In [[abstract indices]], the operator is often written

:<math>\Delta  f = \nabla^a \nabla_a f</math>

provided it is understood implicitly that this trace is in fact the trace of the Hessian ''tensor''.

Because the covariant derivative extends canonically to arbitrary [[tensor]]s, the Laplace–Beltrami operator defined on a tensor ''T'' by
:<math>\Delta  T = g^{ij}\left( \nabla_{X_i}(\nabla_{X_j} T) - \nabla_{\nabla_{X_i}X_j} T\right)</math>
is well-defined.

==Laplace–de Rham operator==
More generally, one can define a Laplacian [[differential operator]] on sections of the bundle of [[differential form]]s on a [[pseudo-Riemannian manifold]]. On a [[Riemannian manifold]] it is an [[elliptic operator]], while on a [[Lorentzian manifold]] it is [[hyperbolic operator|hyperbolic]]. The '''Laplace–de Rham operator''' is defined by

:<math>\Delta = \mathrm{d}\delta + \delta\mathrm{d} = (\mathrm{d}+\delta)^2,\;</math>

where d is the [[exterior derivative]] or differential and ''δ'' is the [[codifferential]], acting as {{nowrap|1=(&minus;1)<sup>''kn''+''n''+1</sup>&lowast;d&lowast;}} on ''k''-forms, where ∗ is the [[Hodge star]]. The first order operator <math>\mathrm{d}+\delta</math> is the Hodge–Dirac operator.<ref>{{cite journal |doi=10.4171/RMI/1041|title=Hodge–Dirac, Hodge–Laplacian and Hodge–Stokes operators in $L^p$ spaces on Lipschitz domains|year=2018|last1=McIntosh|first1=Alan|last2=Monniaux|first2=Sylvie|journal=Revista Matemática Iberoamericana|volume=34|issue=4|pages=1711–1753|arxiv=1608.01797|s2cid=119123242}}</ref>

When computing the Laplace–de Rham operator on a scalar function ''f'', we have {{nowrap|1=''δf'' = 0}}, so that

:<math>\Delta  f = \delta \, \mathrm df.</math>

Up to an overall sign, the Laplace–de Rham operator is equivalent to the previous definition of the Laplace–Beltrami operator when acting on a scalar function; see the proof for details. On functions, the Laplace–de Rham operator is actually the negative of the Laplace–Beltrami operator, as the conventional normalization of the [[codifferential]] assures that the Laplace–de Rham operator is (formally) [[Positive-definite operator|positive definite]], whereas the Laplace–Beltrami operator is typically negative.  The sign is merely a convention, and both are common in the literature.

The Laplace–de Rham operator differs more significantly from the tensor Laplacian restricted to act on skew-symmetric tensors.  Apart from the incidental sign, the two operators differ by a [[Weitzenböck identity]] that explicitly involves the [[Ricci curvature tensor]].

== Examples ==
Many examples of the Laplace–Beltrami operator can be worked out explicitly.

===Euclidean space===
In the usual (orthonormal) [[Cartesian coordinates]] ''x''<sup>''i''</sup> on [[Euclidean space]], the metric is reduced to the Kronecker delta, and one therefore has <math>|g| = 1</math>.  Consequently, in this case

:<math>\Delta  f = \frac{1}{\sqrt{|g|}} \partial_i \sqrt{|g|}\partial^i f = \partial_i \partial^i f</math>

which is the ordinary Laplacian. In [[curvilinear coordinates]], such as [[spherical coordinates|spherical]] or [[cylindrical coordinates]], one obtains [[Laplacian#Coordinate expressions|alternative expressions]].

Similarly, the Laplace–Beltrami operator corresponding to the [[Minkowski metric]] with [[metric signature|signature]] {{nowrap|(&minus; + + +)}} is the [[d'Alembertian]].

===Spherical Laplacian===
The spherical Laplacian is the Laplace–Beltrami operator on the {{nowrap|(''n'' &minus; 1)}}-sphere with its canonical metric of constant [[sectional curvature]]&nbsp;1.  It is convenient to regard the sphere as isometrically embedded into '''R'''<sup>''n''</sup> as the [[unit sphere]] centred at the origin.  Then for a function ''f'' on ''S''<sup>''n''&minus;1</sup>, the spherical Laplacian is defined by
:<math>\Delta _{S^{n-1}}f(x) = \Delta  f(x/|x|)</math>
where ''f''(''x''/|''x''|) is the degree zero homogeneous extension of the function ''f'' to '''R'''<sup>''n''</sup>&nbsp;&minus;&nbsp;{0}, and <math>\Delta</math> is the Laplacian of the ambient Euclidean space.  Concretely, this is implied by the well-known formula for the Euclidean Laplacian in spherical polar coordinates:
:<math>\Delta f = r^{1-n}\frac{\partial}{\partial r}\left(r^{n-1}\frac{\partial f}{\partial r}\right) + r^{-2}\Delta _{S^{n-1}}f.</math>

More generally, one can formulate a similar trick using the [[normal bundle]] to define the Laplace–Beltrami operator of any Riemannian manifold isometrically embedded as a hypersurface of Euclidean space.

One can also give an intrinsic description of the Laplace–Beltrami operator on the sphere in a [[normal coordinates|normal coordinate system]].  Let {{nowrap|(''ϕ'', ''ξ'')}} be spherical coordinates on the sphere with respect to a particular point ''p'' of the sphere (the "north pole"), that is geodesic polar coordinates with respect to ''p''.  Here ''ϕ'' represents the latitude measurement along a unit speed geodesic from ''p'', and ''ξ'' a parameter representing the choice of direction of the geodesic in ''S''<sup>''n''&minus;1</sup>. Then the spherical Laplacian has the form:
:<math>\Delta _{S^{n-1}} f(\xi,\phi) = (\sin\phi)^{2-n} \frac{\partial}{\partial \phi}\left((\sin\phi)^{n-2}\frac{\partial f}{\partial \phi}\right) + (\sin\phi)^{-2}\Delta _\xi f</math>
where <math>\Delta _\xi</math> is the Laplace&ndash;Beltrami operator on the ordinary unit {{nowrap|(''n'' &minus; 2)}}-sphere.  In particular, for the ordinary 2-sphere using standard notation for polar coordinates we get:
:<math>\Delta _{S^{2}} f(\theta,\phi) = (\sin\phi)^{-1} \frac{\partial}{\partial \phi}\left(\sin\phi\frac{\partial f}{\partial \phi}\right) + (\sin\phi)^{-2} \frac{\partial^2}{\partial \theta^2}f</math>

===Hyperbolic space===
A similar technique works in [[hyperbolic space]].  Here the hyperbolic space ''H''<sup>''n''&minus;1</sup> can be embedded into the ''n'' dimensional [[Minkowski space]], a real vector space equipped with the quadratic form
:<math>q(x) = x_1^2 - x_2^2-\cdots - x_n^2.</math>
Then ''H''<sup>''n-1''</sup> is the subset of the future null cone in Minkowski space given by
:<math>H^{n-1} = \{ x \mid q(x) = 1, x_1>1\}. \, </math>
Then
:<math>\Delta _{H^{n-1}} f = \left. \Box f\left(x/q(x)^{1/2}\right) \right| _{H^{n-1}}</math>
Here <math>f(x/q(x)^{1/2})</math> is the degree zero homogeneous extension of ''f'' to the interior of the future null cone and {{math|□}} is the [[wave operator]]
:<math>\Box = \frac{\partial^2}{\partial x_1^2} - \cdots - \frac{\partial^2}{\partial x_n^2}.</math>

The operator can also be written in polar coordinates.  Let {{nowrap|(''t'', ''ξ'')}} be spherical coordinates on the sphere with respect to a particular point ''p'' of ''H''<sup>''n''&minus;1</sup> (say, the center of the [[Poincaré disc]]).  Here ''t'' represents the hyperbolic distance from ''p'' and ''ξ'' a parameter representing the choice of direction of the geodesic in ''S''<sup>''n''&minus;2</sup>. Then the hyperbolic Laplacian has the form:
:<math>\Delta _{H^{n-1}} f(t,\xi) = \sinh(t)^{2-n} \frac{\partial}{\partial t}\left(\sinh(t)^{n-2}\frac{\partial f}{\partial t}\right) + \sinh(t)^{-2}\Delta _\xi f</math>
where <math>\Delta _\xi</math> is the Laplace&ndash;Beltrami operator on the ordinary unit (''n''&nbsp;&minus;&nbsp;2)-sphere.  In particular, for the hyperbolic plane using standard notation for polar coordinates we get:
:<math>\Delta _{H^{2}} f(r,\theta) = \sinh(r)^{-1} \frac{\partial}{\partial r}\left(\sinh(r)\frac{\partial f}{\partial r}\right) + \sinh(r)^{-2} \frac{\partial^2}{\partial \theta^2}f</math>
